records.value:
Lesson 1 — "Why Did the Stool Fall?" (Moment of a Force)
Students observe the anchoring phenomenon (Jiko stool toppling vs. staying upright) and record initial predictions. They are introduced to the concept of the turning effect of a force — the moment — and meet the formula Moment = Force × Perpendicular Distance. They calculate moments for simple scenarios (e.g., pushing open a school gate at different distances from the hinge) and post their first "I notice / I wonder" questions on the Driving Question Board. The cumulative model begins: a diagram of the stool with force arrows.

Lesson 2 — "Turning Forces" (Moment of a Force, from measurements)
Students revisit their predictions and measure how the turning effect of the same mass grows with its distance from a pivot on a metre rule. They derive and apply M = F × d in Kenyan contexts (school gate, handcart), calculate the moment of the jerrycan about the stool's leg and see that a load over the legs turns the stool back while a load beyond the leg tries to turn it over. The cumulative model gains moment-arm annotations. The lesson ends by asking where the stool's own weight acts.

Lesson 3 — "Where Is the 'Balance Point' Hiding?" (Centre of Gravity and States of Equilibrium)
Students determine the centre of gravity of regular shapes (rectangular cardboard) and irregular shapes (cardboard cut-outs of a stool profile and a sufuria lid) by the plumb-line suspension method, and test towers of blocks to see when they topple. They define stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium from their evidence and link the toppling condition (vertical line through the centre of gravity outside the base of support) to the stool. The cumulative model gains a centre-of-gravity marker and a tipping line.

Lesson 4 — "The Principle of Moments" (Balancing on a Bao Plank)
Students investigate the Principle of Moments experimentally using a metre rule, a pencil pivot and improvised masses (bags of beans, coins). They tabulate clockwise and anti-clockwise moments, identify the pattern, state the Principle, and apply it to quantitative problems including a traditional Kenyan see-saw (bao plank across a log) and the toppling and restoring moments of the narrow and wide stools. The cumulative model gains moment arms and a balance-condition label.

Lesson 5 — "How Do Engineers Keep Things From Falling?" (Factors Affecting Stability and Real-Life Applications)
Students investigate how lowering the centre of gravity (adding clay to the base of a tall cardboard box) and widening the base (adjusting cardboard flaps) each independently increase stability. They connect findings to real engineering contexts: crane design, double-decker bus geometry, and why maize sacks are stacked in an interlocking pattern. A case-study card on a tower-crane accident is analysed using moment and stability principles. The cumulative model is updated with stability-factor labels and an engineering example inset.

Lesson 6 — "Can We Explain and Predict Toppling?" (Consolidation, Model Finalisation, and DQB Review)
Students return to the full anchoring phenomenon and all supporting phenomena, using their completed cumulative model to write a full scientific explanation of when and why objects topple or remain stable. The Driving Question Board is reviewed: each posted question is answered with evidence from the unit. Students present their models in groups, peer-assess using a co-constructed rubric, and reflect on career connections. A summative problem set (including a jerrycan-on-stool moment calculation) is completed individually to assess mastery of learning outcomes.

records.why: With a single mass on a rule balanced at its centre, the rule always tips down on that side (the rule cannot be 'slightly' tipped), so the recorded 'balanced / tips slightly / tips strongly' could not be observed. With a fixed 500 g reference mass at 30 cm on the other side, moments are 500 g × 30 cm = 15 000 g·cm; a 500 g mass at 10 cm or 20 cm gives 5 000 or 10 000 g·cm (right side down), at 30 cm equal (balance), at 40 or 50 cm 20 000 or 25 000 g·cm (left side down). A water bottle or packet of sugar of about 500 g is a low-cost substitute for a 500 g mass.
records.old: one 500 g mass, and a printed data table. Task: Place the 500 g mass at 10 cm from the pivot, then 20 cm, 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm from the pivot. At each position, students observe whether the rule tips and record in the table: (a) the distance from pivot in cm, (b) a qualitative observation (balanced / tips slightly / tips strongly), and (c) a sketch showing the mass position and the direction the rule tips.
records.new: two 500 g masses (or two 500 ml water bottles filled with water, tied on with string), and a printed data table. Task: Hang the first 500 g mass (the reference mass) at 30 cm from the pivot on the RIGHT and leave it there. Hang the second 500 g mass on the LEFT at 10 cm from the pivot, then 20 cm, 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm. At each position, students observe which side of the rule goes down and record in the table: (a) the distance of the left mass from the pivot in cm, (b) the observation (left side down / right side down / balanced), and (c) a sketch showing both masses and the direction the rule tips. Expected result: the right side goes down at 10 cm and 20 cm, the rule balances at 30 cm, and the left side goes down at 40 cm and 50 cm.

By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) define the moment of a force and calculate moments in given situations,
b) state and apply the Principle of Moments to solve problems involving balanced systems,
c) state the conditions necessary for a body to be in equilibrium under the action of parallel forces,
d) determine the centre of gravity of regular and irregular objects experimentally,
e) explain the three states of equilibrium (stable, unstable, and neutral) with relevant examples,
f) investigate how the base area and position of the centre of gravity affect the stability of objects,

value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Defines the terms and states the condition mostly correctly, applying it to the stool with some gaps.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses centre of gravity with other ideas, or does not link the vertical line to the base of support.

value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains the phenomenon using most key ideas but the chain of reasoning has a missing link.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Describes what happened without explaining why, or uses ideas incorrectly.
